assessment.1. Nature of the complaint and existence: There was a clear interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression. He was fined for contempt of court because of statements contained in a written objection lodged in pending enforcement proceedings, and the fine was ultimately upheld, though reduced, and later paid (see paragraphs 10-17). A financial penalty imposed on a lawyer for statements made while representing himself and others in judicial proceedings is capable of discouraging robust advocacy and therefore falls within Article 10.

assessment.2. Context of the speech: The speech was made by a lawyer in a procedural submission challenging a refusal to enforce a judgment concerning the applicant’s status as a city councillor and related electoral rights (see paragraphs 8-11). The statements were harsh and sarcastic, describing the court’s approach as "pen-pushing", referring to "legal geniuses", "supreme nonsense", possible "malice" or lack of knowledge, and even abuse of function (see paragraph 11). However, the remarks were closely linked to criticism of the reasoning and functioning of the enforcement court in that case, rather than to the judge’s private life. This is important because the Court affords strong protection to lawyers’ speech when they comment on the administration of justice and defend their clients’ interests, while also requiring them to show a degree of professional restraint (see nos. 31611/96, 29369/10, 73797/01).

assessment.3. Lawfulness and legitimate aim: The interference appears to have been prescribed by law, namely Articles 33 and 51 of the Enforcement Procedure Act, which allowed courts to fine persons who offended the court and fixed the available range of fines (see paragraphs 20-21). It also pursued legitimate aims under Article 10 § 2, namely protecting the authority of the judiciary and the reputation of judges and courts; those aims are expressly recognised in domestic constitutional law as well (see paragraph 19). The decisive issue is therefore whether the sanction was necessary in a democratic society.

assessment.4. Applicable standards on lawyers’ crit: The Court’s case-law accepts that lawyers have a special role as intermediaries in the administration of justice and must be able to defend their clients effectively, even by using strong criticism of judicial actors where this relates to the case and has a sufficient factual basis (see nos. 31611/96, 29369/10). At the same time, lawyers may be sanctioned for gravely insulting or disruptive conduct that undermines the authority of the courts, especially in the courtroom itself (see no. 73797/01). The proportionality analysis therefore turns on the link between the remarks and the case, the forum and audience, the tone used, the reasons given by the domestic courts, and the severity of the sanction.

assessment.5. Contribution to debate and limited di: Although the applicant’s objection primarily served his own litigation interests, it also touched on the functioning of the judiciary and the enforcement of judicial decisions, matters that carry public-interest weight (see paragraphs 8-11). Moreover, the impugned expressions were made in a written objection within court proceedings, not in the media or in a public campaign. Their circulation was therefore very limited. That considerably reduced any possible impact on public confidence in the judiciary. This distinguishes the case from situations where a lawyer publicly attacks judges before a broad audience.

assessment.6. Tone of the remarks and their connect: The applicant’s language was undoubtedly intemperate and discourteous. Some phrases could reasonably be viewed as excessive. Still, the statements were directed at the court’s legal approach, professional competence and handling of the enforcement request in the very proceedings at issue (see paragraph 11). The domestic courts treated them essentially as pure insult, but did not seriously examine whether they were value judgments tied to the disputed ruling, whether they had some factual basis in the applicant’s legal disagreement, or whether the applicant’s rhetoric, though exaggerated, remained within the bounds of adversarial argument. The applicant expressly argued that he was criticising the quality and lawfulness of the judicial work, not making personal attacks unrelated to the case (see paragraph 13).

assessment.7. Relevance and sufficiency of the dome: The reasons given domestically appear insufficient. The first-instance court relied on the insulting character of the wording and on the applicant’s professional status as a lawyer (see paragraph 12). The appellate court added that he had intended to belittle the court and had denied its expertise, thereby damaging its reputation (see paragraph 14). But neither court balanced the competing interests in a Convention-compliant way: they did not assess the limited audience of the pleading, the connection between the remarks and the legal dispute, the distinction between criticism of judicial reasoning and gratuitous personal abuse, or the chilling effect of sanctioning a lawyer for written submissions. The Constitutional Court then merely endorsed the lower courts in very general terms (see paragraph 17). Such reasoning is weaker than what Article 10 requires in cases involving criticism of the judiciary by a lawyer (see nos. 31611/96, 29369/10).

assessment.8. Proportionality of the sanction: The fine was initially RSD 100,000 and then reduced to RSD 50,000, which the applicant eventually paid (see paragraphs 12, 14, 16). Even if not extremely severe, it was still a real pecuniary penalty imposed for statements made in a court pleading. Such a sanction can deter lawyers from defending clients vigorously or from criticising judicial conduct in future cases. Less restrictive responses were available, especially given the absence of public dissemination and the fact that the remarks did not disrupt a hearing. Unlike the circumstances addressed in no. 73797/01, this was not an immediate courtroom confrontation threatening the orderly conduct of proceedings.

assessment.9. Overall conclusion: Balancing the applicant’s role as a lawyer, the close link between the remarks and the impugned decision, the limited circulation of the statements, and the chilling effect of a monetary penalty against the need to protect judicial authority, the domestic courts do not appear to have shown a pressing social need for the sanction. Their reasons were not sufficiently relevant and sufficient, and the interference was disproportionate. The more likely outcome is therefore a finding of a violation of Article 10.
